findings.claim: The lesson names the doctrine 'creator ex nihilo' throughout (description, content_html, conclusion_html, practice_questions, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions and glossary_terms).
findings.truth: The specification's named concept is 'creation ex nihilo' (Component 1 Theme 1 content and concept list). 'Creator ex nihilo' is not the term the paper will use, and it is not correct Latin for the doctrine. The meaning taught is right; only the term is wrong.
findings.evidence: spec lines 3532 and 3646 - 'the concept of creation ex nihilo as expressed in the writing of St Augustine' and the concept list bullet 'creation ex nihilo'

findings.claim: 'Augustine and Aquinas are named scholars in this specification ... Aquinas for human nature as essentially good.'
findings.truth: Aquinas is not named anywhere in the Route B content. The named thinkers for Component 1 are St Augustine of Hippo, St Catherine of Siena and Pope John Paul II. Aquinas appears only in the Route A content, which these candidates do not sit. Natural Law is a Route B concept, so Aquinas remains useful background.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Aquinas' occurs once, at line 546, inside the Route A content (Route B content is sections 2.4-2.6, lines 3465-4300); Route B named thinkers at lines 3532, 3552, 3560

findings.claim: 'taught in the Lord's Prayer that forgiving others and receiving God's forgiveness are inseparably linked (Matthew 6:5-13)'
findings.truth: The explicit teaching that the two are linked is Matthew 6:14-15, the verses the specification itself cites. The Lord's Prayer is Matthew 6:9-13. Citing 6:5-13 stops one verse short of the teaching being described.
findings.evidence: spec line ~3960 (Theme 4, Sin and Forgiveness): 'Christian teachings about forgiveness, including interpretations of teachings: Matthew 18:21-22, Matthew 6: 14-15'

findings.truth: 'An absolutist'. SPaG is assessed on this qualification, so the lesson prose should model it.
findings.evidence: grammar; spec lines 4350-4356 confirm SPaG is assessed in Components 1 and 2

findings.claim: Virtue ethics is taught as one of the 'three main approaches to ethics' that Catholic moral teaching draws on, and the exam tip says 'Virtue ethics is particularly important here'.
findings.truth: The Route B concept list names absolutism and relativism (Theme 4) and Natural Law and conscience (Theme 2). Virtue ethics is not a named concept on this route; the only virtue reference is 'the role of suffering in the development of the virtues'. Options: (a) leave it, on the grounds that it is genuine Catholic moral theology and supports the Natural Law material; (b) keep the teaching but soften the exam tip so a student does not revise it as set content. Recommendation: (b) - the content is sound, the exam-priority claim is not.
findings.evidence: spec concept lists at lines 3776-3786 (Theme 2) and 4080-4090 (Theme 4); 'virtue' appears only at line 3738
findings.ruling: Leave: coverage/scope gap recorded as a follow-up build item (not a surgical fix).

findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners do. House rule: no fabricated examiner claims. Replace with concrete advice about the answer itself.
findings.evidence: house rule in the checker brief

findings.claim: Knowledge check 5 gives Corpus Christi's meaning as 'A holy day of obligation celebrating the body and blood of Christ'.
findings.truth: Corpus Christi is not a holy day of obligation in England and Wales; it was transferred to the following Sunday in 2006 and was not restored in the 2016 review. The lesson's own content says exactly this, so the answer key contradicts the lesson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Holy day of obligation' - England and Wales list is Epiphany, Ascension, Ss Peter and Paul, Assumption, All Saints, Christmas; Corpus Christi is not on it

findings.claim: 'Several major solemnities are holy days of obligation ... These include Corpus Christi (... in Britain, Corpus Christi is transferred to the following Sunday and is not a separate holy day of obligation), the feast of St Peter and St Paul ...'
findings.truth: The sentence lists Corpus Christi as a holy day of obligation and then denies it in the same breath. Corpus Christi should sit outside the list.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Holy day of obligation' (England and Wales)

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Name one British Catholic pilgrimage site mentioned in the specification.' Answer: 'Holywell (North Wales) or the Marian Shrine of Cardigan.'
findings.truth: Neither Holywell nor Cardigan appears in this specification. The only pilgrimage site it names for Catholic Christianity is Lourdes. The answer is also a two-item 'or' list, which the flashcard validator disallows.
findings.evidence: spec line 3754 - 'the meaning and significance of pilgrimage for Catholics as a response to human suffering, with particular reference to Lourdes'; 'Holywell' and 'Cardigan' return no matches

findings.claim: The Sacred Triduum is given as Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Holy Saturday.
findings.truth: The Roman Missal's Paschal Triduum begins with the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday and closes with Evening Prayer on Easter Sunday, so it includes Easter Sunday. Most GCSE resources use the lesson's three days, so a student would not be marked down. Recorded, not edited.
findings.evidence: General Norms for the Liturgical Year, nn. 18-21

findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners do. House rule: no fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: Of the Second Vatican Council: 'It produced four major documents.'
findings.truth: The Council produced sixteen documents - four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. The four named in the lesson (Lumen Gentium, Gaudium et Spes, Dei Verbum, Sacrosanctum Concilium) are the four constitutions, which is what the specification means by 'four key documents'.
findings.evidence: spec line 3846 - 'The nature and importance of the Second Vatican Council, its history and four key documents'; Vatican II document list (vatican.va)

findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners do. House rule: no fabricated examiner claims.
findings.evidence: house rule in the checker brief

findings.claim: 'Mendicant orders (Franciscan, Dominican, Carmelite) go into the world to preach and serve - they own no property as communities and historically depended on alms.'
findings.truth: Stated in the present tense this is wrong. The ban on communal property belonged to the original mendicant ideal; mendicant orders today own priories, schools and churches. The sentence already mixes tenses ('own' then 'historically depended').
findings.evidence: history of the mendicant orders; the sentence's own tense clash

findings.claim: Roughly half the lesson - religious life, monastic and mendicant orders, the evangelical counsels, contemplative and apostolic orders - plus three of the six practice questions, teach religious orders as examinable content.
findings.truth: None of this is in the Route B specification. 'Religious order', 'monastic', 'Benedict', 'Francisc', 'vocation' and 'evangelical counsel' return no matches anywhere in Components 1, 2 or 3 for this route. The specification's own Forms and Practices content for these themes is the San Clemente Tree of Life apse mosaic, Faure's Requiem and the funeral rite, the sarcophagus in the Museo Pio Cristiano, the altar and font, and church orientation - none of which the unit covers. Options: (a) leave the lesson as enrichment and accept that a third of its practice is off-spec; (b) keep the Forms half (symbols, Michelangelo, the Rosary), demote religious life to background, and build the missing spec Forms content into the unit. Recommendation: (b), as a rebuild queued separately - it is beyond a surgical edit.
findings.evidence: spec grep over lines 3465-4300: no match for religious orders, monastic, Benedict, Francisc or evangelical counsels; Forms content at lines 3608-3625, 3744-3757, 3860-3880
findings.ruling: Leave: coverage/scope gap recorded as a follow-up build item (not a surgical fix).

findings.claim: 'For describe or explain questions about religious orders, distinguish clearly between monastic ... and mendicant ...'
findings.truth: This promises exam questions on content the specification does not set for this route (see F15). The advice is fine as background; the exam claim is not.
findings.evidence: spec grep - religious orders do not appear in Route B content

summary: Five lessons checked against the Route B content. Doctrine, scripture, Catechism paragraphs, conciliar documents, dates and answer keys are almost all sound; the exam-facing layer is where the errors sit. One HIGH: a knowledge check calls Corpus Christi a holy day of obligation, contradicting the lesson's own text and the England and Wales calendar. Three fabricated examiner claims, a spec term used wrong throughout lesson 1 ('creator' for 'creation' ex nihilo), and half of lesson 5 teaching religious orders that this route does not set.
